feedback: If the child says young should be identical and treats differences as odd, compare several offspring against both parents to establish resemblance-plus-difference as the normal pattern.
If the child attributes every feature to the one parent shown, introduce the second parent as another source of features so the young is a blend of both.

If the child denies plant offspring resemble the parent plant, show young plants grown from the parent's seeds that, once grown, share the parent's leaf shape or flower colour with some variation, paralleling the animal case.
If the child insists young always look like small adults, give examples where young look very different (caterpillar, tadpole) yet are still that species' offspring.
If the child says the resemblance is because they live together, redirect to the parents as the source of the shared features.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who holds the idea can name both the inherited similarities and the individual differences, and (toward Year 6) explain that young animals, and plants grown from seed, usually get a mix of features from two parents rather than being a copy of one.
learnerActions: Match babies to parents and explain the feature that justified each match.
Answer whether siblings from the same parents are identical or varying, and give a reason.
Find the 'odd one out' difference within a litter or seedling group.

Respond to a reasoning prompt: a puppy has its mother's floppy ears and brown fur, but a differently shaped tail and a white patch she lacks — are the puppy and its mum exactly the same, or not, and why?
activities.title: Check: like but not identical
